lesson.title: The published catalogue of liturgical books

readings.title: Hapgood’s catalogue of service books
readings.locator: Preface, printed pp. v–vi: complete numbered catalogue 1–12 and the intervening Typikon paragraph, with marked omissions of transliterations
readings.text:
A list of the service books which have entered into the composition of my volume will afford some idea of the difficulties of the problem.

(1) The […] or Service Book, which contains most of the fixed portions of the Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil the Great, and of the Presanctified Gifts; also the Litanies and Prayers of Vespers and Matins, together with the Graduals and Benedictions appropriate to all occasions. This is used by the Priest and the Choir.

(2) The […] or Book of the Hours (Horologion), which contains, in addition to the Hours and the Typical Psalms, those fixed portions of Vespers, Compline, Matins, Midnight Service, and so forth, which are used by the singers and the readers; also a selection of Hymns for various occasions.

(3) The Pontifical Service Book […] which contains the fixed portions of the Liturgies above mentioned, as celebrated by a Bishop; together with all the Offices of Ordination, ecclesiastical promotion, the blessing of an antimíns (corporal), and so forth.

(4) The […] or Book of the Eight Tones, which contains the Canons and certain of the Hymns used during Little and Great Vespers, Compline, Midnight Service, and Matins; the Hymn for the Day and the Collect-Hymn from the Canons being used also at the Liturgy on the following morning. There are eight complete sets for each service mentioned, for every day in the week, all during one week being sung in the same Tone.

(5) The Monthly […] in twelve volumes, which contain the order of services for all the fixed days in the year celebrating some special event in the history of the faith or the Church, or commemorating a Saint or Saints. All the […] contain the Prayers for Vespers and Matins, while some have special Prayers for the Hours, Liturgies, Compline, and the Midnight Service.

(6) The volume known as the Anthologion […] contains the Services for the Twelve Great Feasts.

(7) The Fasting Triodion […] contains the variable portions of the services on the movable days which constitute the preparation for the Great Fast (Lent), and during the entire Great Fast. It is so called because the Canons have only Three Odes (or Theme-Songs), instead of the customary nine—practically eight—which are in the Book of the Eight Tones […].

(8) The […] (Flowery Triodion), or […] contains the order of services during Easter-tide, beginning with Easter and ending with Pentecost, including the following day,—Whitsun Monday,—which is the real Pentecost, or Day of the Spirit, Sunday being called Trinity Day.

(9) The […] contains the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles, and the Graduals, Introits and Anthems for the Feasts.

For their guidance in the use of these complicated volumes the ecclesiastics have a volume entitled the […] or Rule, which provides regulations for all possible contingencies.

(10) The Great […] or Book of Needs, which contains all the Sacraments (except the Holy Communion and Ordination),—Baptism, Chrismation, Confession, Matrimony, Unction of the Sick; together with various other services, such as the Reception of Converts from various other Churches, the Tonsure of Monks, the Anointment of the Emperor at his Coronation, and so forth; also private services, such as Prayers at the Birth of a Child, the several Funeral Services, the Consecration of a Church, the Blessing of a New Dwelling, and so forth.

(11) A Book of Te Deums and Prayer Services […] for different occasions.

(12) The […] which contains the Theme-Songs of the Canons, and certain Services of Song in honour of Our Lord, the Birth-giver of God, St. Nicholas, and others.
readings.context: The 1906 compiler’s English descriptions are quoted. Bracketed ellipses mark omitted foreign transliterations, rather than silently replacing them with modern spellings. The named source books and historical service scope belong to that publication.

scripture.text:
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;

Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.

And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.

And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.

And what soever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.

overview.text: Hapgood’s preface explains that her English volume draws on several distinct service books. Some supply fixed prayers; others supply material that changes by weekday, feast, or season. The catalogue helps explain why Orthodox worship cannot be understood as the contents of one small book.

readings.title: How the different books work together

paragraphs.text: The Service Book and Horologion supply fixed material for clergy, singers, and readers; the Pontifical book concerns services involving a bishop. The Book of Eight Tones organizes recurring hymn material, while monthly volumes and feast collections supply commemorations. The Triodion concerns the preparation for Lent and Lent itself, and the following festal collection concerns the Paschal period. The Typikon coordinates their use, while the Book of Needs covers the other sacraments and occasional services listed by Hapgood.
